title: Nobody asked for the sparkle button
text:
Nobody asked for the sparkle button

Products ship with the same AI panel; people hunt for the off switch, and spend has outrun returns. Build features with AI, not AI features.

Open any product you pay for and look at the top right corner. There is a sparkle. Behind it is a panel that slides in from the right, says “Ask anything”, and offers three suggestions you did not ask for. Close it and it comes back after the next update, sometimes with a new name.

I should be the last person to complain. I write code with AI every working day. When I built 131 variations of one button to study hover feedback, a model wrote most of them. My design files are generated from code that AI wrote. I am about as far from a sceptic as a designer gets, and I still spend part of every week looking for the switch that turns a sparkle off.

That is the gap this piece is about. The tools got genuinely good. The products built on top of them mostly did not, because most of them are the same product.

The same product, forty times

Here is the feature. A chat panel, docked right. A text box with a placeholder in the second person. Three suggested prompts written by someone who has never used the app for real work. A sparkle icon, because the sparkle is now the universal sign for “we added it”. It summarises the thing you were already reading. It drafts the thing you were about to write. It answers questions about the page you are on, with a disclaimer that it may be wrong.

I have seen that panel in a notes app, a spreadsheet, a design tool, a mail client, a team chat, a video call, a browser, a photo editor, a slide deck, a calendar, a music player and a bank. Not similar panels. The same panel. If you took the logos off, nobody on the team that built one could pick theirs out.

There is a simple reason it converged. The model vendors sell the same capability to everyone, through the same API, with the same demo. A company that buys the demo and ships it has not designed anything. It has forwarded it. The feature is named after the technology, “AI assistant”, “Copilot”, “Intelligence”, because there is no user goal to name it after. Nobody ever shipped a “database feature”. They shipped search.

None of this is a new observation. In 2023, before most of these panels existed, Amelia Wattenberger wrote Why Chatbots Are Not the Future and showed why a blank text box is the worst way to expose a capable model: it tells you nothing about what it can do. The same year Maggie Appleton published her Language Model Sketchbook, subtitled “or why I hate chatbots”, with three working alternatives, one of them a model that lives in the right-click menu of the document you are writing. The industry read both pieces and shipped the text box anyway.

Forced on, not opted in

The part people actually resent is not that the panel exists. It is that it was turned on for them, and that off is hard to find.

Microsoft is the clearest case because it is the biggest. Copilot went into Notepad, the Snipping Tool, Photos and Widgets, with the button in the toolbar and no plain way to remove it. In March 2026 the company said it would cut back on “unnecessary Copilot entry points”, starting with those four apps, and the head of Windows wrote that Microsoft would be more intentional about where Copilot goes. That is a company admitting, in public, that it had added AI to a text editor without a reason.

The reaction is not confined to grumpy enthusiasts. A Hacker News thread titled “I’m drowning in AI features I never asked for and I hate it” passed three hundred points, and the top complaints were from people who use AI daily by choice: they were objecting to the version they could not decline. Outside the industry it is wider still. In Pew’s June 2025 survey, half of American adults said AI’s growing role in daily life left them more concerned than excited, against one in ten who felt the other way.

Meta went further than Microsoft. In spring 2025 a blue and purple ring appeared in the WhatsApp chat list, then in the search bar, and there was no way to remove it. Meta called the feature optional. You could choose not to tap it. That is the definition of optional a company reaches for when the feature cannot survive a real one.

Every designer knows what a feature that people keep turning off is called. It is a bug with a marketing budget.

What the loop costs

The toggle that resets is a small thing, and that is why it does so much damage. A setting is a promise. The product said “this is yours to decide”, you decided, and an update decided back. The click to fix it costs nothing. What costs is what you learn from it: this product will override me.

Once learned, that rule does not stay on the one feature. Every update becomes something to audit. You stop reading release notes for what is new and start reading them for what has been done to you. People delay updates, pin old versions, and search for “disable” before they search for “how to”. That is the cognitive friction: not the dismissals themselves, but the vigilance they teach. Attention that should go to the work goes to guarding the interface.

Then it moves from the product to the brand. In January 2025 Apple paused its notification summaries for news apps after the feature rewrote a BBC alert into a false claim that a murder suspect had shot himself. The summary was on by default. The mistake was the model’s, but the name on the notification was Apple’s, and the BBC complained to Apple, not to the model. A feature forced on carries the brand on every error it makes.

The last stage is the strangest. In August 2024 the head of Procreate recorded a video to say the app would never add generative AI, and the artists who use it cheered. A promise not to ship a roadmap item went viral. That is what the loop buys, in the end: a market in which the absence of your feature is a selling point for your competitor.

Trust is cheap to lose here for a structural reason. One forced toggle does not teach “this feature is annoying”. It teaches “this company will override me”, and a rule about the company applies to everything it ships next, including the feature that would have been good.

The bill

So why does it keep shipping? Because of what it cost to build the thing underneath.

UBS now estimates the big cloud companies will spend about $4.1 trillion on capital expenditure between 2026 and 2028, after roughly $492 billion in 2025. In 2026 Amazon, Alphabet and Microsoft together are expected to spend 102 percent of their cloud revenue on capex. Every dollar that comes in from cloud goes back out as chips and buildings, and then some.

That money has to come back from somewhere, and the somewhere is us: every product team that buys tokens and every customer who pays for the seat. Which is why the panel is on by default. A feature that is off is a feature nobody is billed for.

Now put that next to what the buyers are getting. MIT’s NANDA group looked at 300 public deployments and interviewed 150 leaders, and found that 95 percent of companies saw no measurable return from their generative AI pilots. The 5 percent that did had integrated the tool into one specific workflow and learned from it. Gartner’s own number is kinder and still bleak: one in five AI initiatives delivers any measurable return, and one in fifty delivers something transformational.

Is this panic?

Not yet, and the word is wrong anyway. Panic is fast. What I see on product teams is slower and more embarrassing: the roadmap has an item called “AI” with no user problem under it, and for the first time someone with a budget is asking what it is for.

The newest version of the item is called an agentic strategy. Everyone has one. Almost nobody who has one can show you a map of how the work in their company actually gets done: who starts a task, what they open, who they wait on, where it stalls. An agent is a worker. You cannot hire a worker for a job you have not described, and the description is the part nobody wrote.

Those are the two halves of the same mistake. The spend assumed demand would appear once the capability existed. The product teams assumed a feature would appear once they had the API. Both skipped the step where you find a person with a goal and ask what would help. That step is called design, and it is the step that got cut because the board wanted the sparkle on the slide by the next quarter.

Jakob Nielsen called this technology the first new UI paradigm in sixty years: you state the outcome you want instead of the steps to get there. Take him at his word and the docked panel looks even stranger. A new paradigm arrived, and the industry gave it the interface of a 1990s support chat.

You can tell which features skipped it. They are the ones named after the technology. They are the ones that are on by default and hard to turn off, because a feature nobody asked for has to be forced to get used. And they are the ones whose success metric is “engagement with the panel” rather than anything the person came to do.

Features with AI, not AI features

I have one rule for my own work, and it has held up: build features with AI, not AI features.

The 131 buttons were a feature built with AI. A person wanted hover feedback that answered a real question. A model wrote the variations in an afternoon so I could spend my time judging them. The person who eventually uses the button sees no sparkle, no panel, no disclaimer. They see a button that behaves well. AI is in the process, not the product.

The reservation card in my last piece is the same. AI writes the states, the long French name, the failed photo, the slow network, so the design is judged in the material it ships in. Nobody on the receiving end has to know a model was involved, and nobody has to opt out of anything.

The sparkle panel is the opposite shape. AI is in the product, and the process that should have come first, finding the goal, never ran.

The ones you do not notice

It is fair to ask what the other kind looks like, so here are four I use, and none of them has a sparkle on it.

Gmail’s Smart Compose, from 2018, is the oldest and still the cleanest. You type, grey text appears ahead of your cursor, you press Tab or you keep typing. There is nothing to open and nothing to close. It is named after what it does, it lives in the box you were already typing in, and it does nothing until you are mid-sentence. Now look at the same inbox in 2026. A “Summarise this email” button sits on top of a three-line message. Same company, same model family, two different shapes, and only one of them was designed from a goal.

Photoshop’s Remove tool is a brush. You paint over the thing you want gone and it is gone. It sits beside the healing brush it replaces, in the toolbar where that job has always been. The model is in the tool and the name is not.

Figma’s rename layers command takes a chore nobody wanted and turns it into one keystroke. The result is a list of sensible names in the panel you were already looking at. No chat, no suggestions, no “Ask anything”.

Descript’s remove filler words is the same shape for audio. One command, the ums are gone, and you are back in the transcript.

Emily Campbell’s Shape of AI catalogues the interface patterns that have emerged around models, and it is worth an afternoon. What strikes me reading it is that the patterns that work, the ones she files under inputs and governors, are mostly invoked from inside the work, and the sparkle panel is not a pattern at all. It is a place to put the patterns you have not designed yet.

What they share is easy to list. Each is named after a verb. Each lives where the work already happens. Each is invoked, so there is nothing to turn off, because it does nothing until you ask. And each solves a problem a person could have described before the model existed. The model made the solution possible. It did not pick the problem.

Four questions before you ship one

If an AI feature is on your roadmap, these are the questions I would want answered before a line of it gets built. They are ordinary product questions. That is the point.

  • Who asked? Not “would users like this”, but which person, on which task, got stuck in a way this unsticks. If the answer is “the board”, stop.
  • What is it named after? If the name is the technology, there is no goal in it yet. Rename it after what it does for the person. If you can’t, you don’t have a feature.
  • Would you ship it off by default? If the feature only earns its place when forced on, it has no place. The people who want it will find the switch; the ones who don’t should never have to.
  • Would it survive at cost price? The tokens are subsidised today by that $4.1 trillion. Price the feature as if they weren’t. If it dies, it was never worth more than its marketing.

Most sparkle panels fail all four. The good AI features I have seen, and there are some, pass all four and have no sparkle on them, because they were designed the way everything else was: from a person with a goal, backwards.

In the room

The questions are easy to agree with and hard to use. I lead design at a fintech and report to the CEO, and I have no budget authority either. Here is what has worked for me when the roadmap arrives with “AI” on it and no problem under it.

Do not argue with the strategy. “Should we have an agentic strategy” is a yes or no question with a board behind the yes, and you lose it in the room. Change the question to “which job”. Nobody with a strategy can object to being asked where it applies.

Volunteer for the map. Offer two weeks to document how three real tasks get done today: who starts them, what they open, who they wait on, where they stall. Leadership rarely refuses, because it is cheap and it looks like progress on the strategy. The map is where an agent either finds a job or does not, and you are the one holding it. You have moved the decision from a slide to evidence without saying no to anyone.

Bring the four questions as a form, not an objection. A one-page brief that every AI item fills in before it gets built. Nobody can argue against filling in a form. Items that cannot fill it in die quietly, and nobody has to be the person who killed them.

Rename it in the ticket. “AI assistant” becomes “Draft the reply” or “Find the duplicate”. When there is no verb to rename it after, that shows in the ticket, and the product manager notices before you have to point.

Price it. Ask what the tokens cost per seat at list price and put that beside the price of the seat. You do not need budget authority to ask a question whose answer has a currency sign on it.

Propose the opt-in version as the experiment. Ship it off by default and measure who turns it on and keeps it on. That is a real signal, and it is the version you wanted anyway. If leadership insists on default-on, ask for an off switch that is one tap away and survives updates. That is a fallback you can usually win, and it protects the thing the loop above destroys.

And when you lose, lose well. Ship it, instrument it with a task metric rather than panel opens, and bring the number back in a quarter. Being right in a quarter beats being right in the meeting, and it is the only kind of right that changes the next roadmap.

The sparkle is a confession

Nobody chose the icon on purpose, either. Fast Company traced how the sparkle took over AI and found no first use, only a drift from the emoji people used when they wrote about models to the glyph on the button, because it read as magic and nobody had a better idea. A sparkle icon tells you two things. The company has a model, and it did not know what to do with it. It is a label that says “AI goes here” in a product where nobody found the place.

The investment will sort itself out or it won’t. I am not an economist, and the people who are don’t agree. But the product side is not a mystery, and it is not a bubble. It is a generation of teams that were handed a capability and told to ship it, and skipped the part of the job that would have told them where.

Find the person. Find the goal. Build the feature with the AI, then take the sparkle off. Nobody will miss it.

title: Where to draw the line before AI reaches professional users
text:
Where to draw the line before AI reaches professional users

Six questions to ask for whether a conversational layer will speed experts up or quietly put a keyboard between them and the work they already know.

Nearly every B2B application I’ve seen has a chat box on it. Sometimes a sidebar, sometimes a rebuild where the prompt becomes the front door.

The feature is usually well designed and has an element of sparkly craft in it, because that’s how we are defining craft in AI now, right?

The question underneath it — who is this for, and what were they doing thirty seconds ago, how long have they been doing it in their career — usually goes unanswered.

That question matters more in professional applications than anywhere else, because these users aren’t visitors, they expert users in very specific domains; they have spent decades learning their domain and their software.

I’ve spend decades, literally, watching them and have come to the conclusion that some use cases should never be replaced by AI because it will never beat them.

They’re a claims adjuster on file 82 of the week, an attorney who has read 10,000 contracts and knows the difference between assignment and change of control is just a few words they wrote in a contract 7 years ago and reuse the same pattern today, a supply planner who knows every exception code by heart. They open the same six screens every morning and know exactly where everything lives.

For them, conversation is a detour through a mine laden text field for a group of users that have off the charts cognitive limits because they’ve been in their domain, forever.

I know, I’ve seen it — in real time.

These UX decisions are downstream of one missing step: nobody drew the line first and that line is written in pencil. The reality is that where the line is for a professional application is a bit smudged, but we still have to draw it, especially in the time of AI.

Here are six considerations that tell you where the line belongs.

Does It Break Existing Skills?

An expert has built a skill inside your product — keyboard paths, saved views, the workaround they invented in 2019 they have written on post it notes shaves 90 seconds off a daily task.

I’ve seen that last one much more than I would like.

None of this shows up in your analytics, and all of it gets written off the day you replace the surface it lives on.

The write-off is bigger than it looks, because they aren’t only learning your new screen, they’re learning a new way of working. Jakob Nielsen argues AI is the “first new UI paradigm in 60 years”, after batch processing in 1945 and command-based interaction in 1964. An industry teaches a paradigm slowly, and your users pay tuition to every product that tries.

You’ll hear the resistance called sunk cost fallacy, usually as grounds to override it.

Wrong label.

A sunk cost shouldn’t touch the next decision. The months your user spent learning your product aren’t spent — they’re invested, and they pay out every morning, and they won’t even upgrade software to change their patterns.

The users are protecting an asset. The roadmap is protecting a decision.

The fallacy sits on the other side of the table. A team that funded a chat surface for two quarters, watched adoption stall and shipped it anyway is running the pattern Barry Staw documented in “Knee-Deep in the Big Muddy”: people commit the most resources to a failing course precisely when they caused the earlier losses.

The expertise reversal effect names the mechanism: support that helps beginners turns costly for anyone who already knows the domain. A conversational layer is scaffolding, a gift on day one and an obstruction in year four.

For example, natural language might seem cool, but the recruiter or lawyer that has 400 saved searches? They’ll want the knobs and dials because they know better than AI.

The bar isn’t “better.”

Say the multiple out loud: three times faster, or something the old path couldn’t do at all. If you can’t name a number, ship it beside the old path so you can learn.

Graphical interfaces kept the command line for 20 years, and the people who needed it never stopped using it.

Is The Chat Only for Novices?

Conversation solves recall.

If you don’t know a system, every menu is a vocabulary test you’re failing in public, which is why most enterprise applications are information architecture mine fields. Type a sentence instead and the burden moves to the machine. That’s a real improvement, and it’s why chat lands so well in a demo — demos are always someone’s first day.

Tesler’s law names what’s actually happening: complexity is conserved. Every system has an irreducible amount of it, and the only question is who absorbs it.

Chat doesn’t remove the complexity of your product, it relocates it and leverages the system to help with AI.

For someone who doesn’t know the system that’s a good trade — the machine takes the part they can’t carry. For the expert it runs backwards. They absorbed it years ago, in the form of the field name and the status code, and the prompt hands it back to them as a phrasing problem.

Direct manipulation solved the same problem from the other side. Ben Shneiderman’s 1983 formulation, still the cleanest definition anyone has written, put objects on screen where you could see them, act on them and undo what you did. Recognition instead of recall.

  • For the novice, the prompt is a rescue.
  • For the expert, it’s a translation layer over a system they already speak fluently, no matter how complex.

NN/g calls the novice’s version of this the articulation barrier — people know what they want, can’t phrase it, and get generic results back. Experts have the reverse problem. They know the field name, the status code, the exact filter, and are much faster with it.

Asking them to describe it in a sentence doesn’t lower a barrier, it builds one in many cases. Test accordingly.

Do Users Need to See the Whole Set?

Here’s what filters do that a prompt can’t: When an adjuster narrows a queue to 12 open files, they don’t just get 12 files, they learn there are 12 and not 400, that three are past SLA, and that the pattern looks like a Tuesday last November.

None of that was the question, all of it is the answer and scanning is diagnosis.

Filtering is a hypothesis you can run in half a second and abandon just as fast, which is why experts sweep through six before committing to one. A chat response hands back a result without the shape of what surrounds it.

A chat answer tells you what you asked for; a screen tells you what you should have asked.

Linus Lee made the harder version of this point in 2022: conversations are a bad way to keep track of information, because the state you need ends up in scroll back instead of in front of you.

Screens also carry something transcripts don’t — a shared model. Two people looking at the same view see the same thing, and they can point. A conversation is private by construction, so every user builds their own path and nobody can audit it.

Fine for a consumer app but a real problem in an operations team of 40. That’s why AI search may not be the answer.

Does It Slow Experts Down?

METR ran a randomized trial with experienced open-source developers on their own repositories and found them 19% slower when allowed to use AI tools. The part that should worry you more: they expected a 24% speedup going in and still believed they’d gotten one coming out. They could not feel it happening.

Small sample, one kind of work, so don’t over-read it. It rhymes with the largest field experiment we have. Dell’Acqua, Mollick, Lakhani and their co-authors put 758 consultants through the jagged technological frontier study: inside AI’s capability, subjects were 25.1% faster at higher quality; on tasks just outside it, 19% less likely to be correct than the control.

Expertise is already compression. A prompt asks the expert to decompress it into English so the machine can compress it back.

Watch a partner who has drafted the same indemnity clause 200 times. They don’t compose it, they recall it, and the recall is close to instant, nuance is more real than AI understands, and they have to write it in the spirit of the original language.

The prompt-read-correct loop costs them more than that and leaves them less certain than when they started, because now they’re checking someone else’s work instead of trusting their own.

The model isn’t bad. They’re very good, and the interface asked them to slow to the speed of a sentence.

How Hard Is It to Verify?

In professional work an answer isn’t finished when it appears. It’s finished when someone has checked it and will put their name on it. That cost never shows up in the demo.

Stanford researchers tested the purpose-built legal research tools — the ones sold specifically as grounded and reliable — and found Lexis+ AI and Thomson Reuters’ tools hallucinating between 17% and 33% of the time.

Better than a general chatbot.

Nowhere near good enough for an associate to stop reading every citation, which means the associate is still reading every citation.

The more an output has to be defended to a third party, the worse a chat box performs as the place to make it.

Chat is structurally poor at supporting the check. It returns prose, and prose flattens the difference between what was retrieved and what was generated. A filtered result is auditable by construction — the query sits in the chips above the table, and anyone can rerun it.

Ask who has to defend the output: the further an answer travels, the more the surface has to show its work.

Where Should the Work Go?

None of this means don’t build it. It means work has three destinations and only one of them is a chat box.

Routine Tasks Stay in the Interface

The first destination is the queue somebody works 200 times a day, the saved views, the keyboard path they could walk in the dark. Repetition is what buys speed here, and the speed is the product.

Cost runs the same direction and catches teams out: a click costs nothing to serve, while a prompt against the core loop bills you every time someone does what they used to do for free — which is why cost heads Gartner’s list of reasons these projects get cancelled.

Put a text field in front of the daily queue and you’ve charged your best users a tax to use their own product.

Rare Tasks Go to Chat

The second is the long tail nobody would design a screen for. Which of these 400 contracts have a change-of-control clause and a non-standard liability cap. One-offs that cross the whole schema and become a ticket to an analyst who answers in three days. Answers that are anomalies deep in the financial analysis.

That’s where conversation is worth real money, because the alternative isn’t a filter because it’s a wait, and a question asked once a quarter is worth paying per call for.

Call it the ticket test.

If the user would have filed a ticket, chat is competing against three days and the bar is low. If they would have clicked, it’s competing with muscle memory, and muscle memory is undefeated.

Ongoing Tasks Go to an Agent

The third destination is the one teams keep missing, and it isn’t a conversation at all.

  • A contract arrives with a non-standard cap.
  • A shipment slips its window.
  • An account’s usage drops three weeks running.

Nobody needs to type a question about any of these, because the system already knows. That work belongs to an ambient agent running against the same data your screens display, interrupting only when a person has to decide something.

The idea isn’t new. Christopher Noessel called these systems agentive a decade ago in “Designing Agentive Technology”, and Golden Krishna argued for background processes over screens in “The Best Interface Is No Interface” in 2015. The models are finally good enough to make it work.

Chat waits to be asked. An ambient agent already knows.

Chat is pull and needs the user to know a question exists. Ambient is push and needs the system to be right about what deserves attention, which is the harder problem and the better product. Get it wrong and you’ve built a notification nobody trusts, so tune for precision and let the agent stay quiet. Get it right and it does the scanning nobody can do at 3 a.m., then hands back a filtered queue — which is to say it ends where the interface begins.

Conclusion

The line has nothing to do with how you feel about conversation. It’s a question about who’s standing in front of the screen and how many times they’ve done this before.

The truth:

  • Novices need language —they don’t have the map nor the dictionary.
  • Experts have the map — they built it, they maintain it, and every screen in your product is a landmark on it.

Handing them a text box asks them to give up the map and describe the terrain instead, to someone who’s never been there and occasionally makes places up.

So run the checklist before you run the sprint. Answer the five questions honestly, on real usage data rather than the demo in your head, and the roadmap sorts itself.

What’s left is a smaller chat feature than the one you were planning, aimed at work your users currently can’t do at all, sitting beside an interface you didn’t have to apologize for and an agent quietly working the queue while nobody’s watching. That’s a better product than a prompt on top of everything. It’s also harder to demo, which is most of the reason it doesn’t get built.

Checklist

The six tests reduce to five questions. They’re abstract on purpose — they should still work after the next model release, and the one after that. Saleema Amershi, Mihaela Vorvoreanu and their colleagues at Microsoft Research validated 18 guidelines for human-AI interaction against 20 shipping products in 2019. These five are narrower, and only settle whether a conversation belongs in front of an expert at all.

  • How well does this person already know the system? Everything else follows from this one. Language helps whoever lacks the map and gets in the way of whoever drew it.
  • Is this task routine, rare, or continuous? Routine work belongs to the interface, where repetition buys speed. Rare work belongs to conversation, because nobody was ever going to build a screen for it. Continuous work belongs to an agent that watches and interrupts, because nobody should have to remember to ask.
  • Does the user need an answer, or the shape of the whole set? Retrieval is a question with a reply. Diagnosis is a question about what surrounds the reply, and it needs a surface that shows the surroundings.
  • Who is faster here, and who is more certain? Speed without certainty isn’t speed. It’s a cost that shows up later, in the time it takes someone to trust the output enough to sign their name to it.
  • Is it worth what switching costs? Every new path bills the user for the old one they’d already mastered. If you can’t say plainly how much better this is, leave the old path where it is and let them choose.

Action Items

  • Put chat where the tickets are. Pull 90 days of requests your customers sent to analysts and operations; that queue is a validated feature list with volumes already attached.
  • Give every answer a screen to land on. Render results as a filtered view the user can adjust, save and share, so the conversation hands off to the interface instead of replacing it.
  • Measure verification time, not generation time. Track how long it takes a user to trust an answer enough to act on it, and whether that number is falling.
  • Find the alerts nobody set up. Ask your users what they check by hand every morning, and what they wish someone had told them last week. Each answer is an ambient agent with a job and an audience already attached that wants to be helped.
  • Watch the fallback ratio. Keep the clicking path and track which one users reach for. That ratio is what they actually think of the feature, and it won’t match what they say in a research session.

title: Entering Atomic Design from the screen
text:
Entering Atomic Design from the screen

You don’t always have to build from atoms. Sometimes, you need to discover them.

Atomic Design is one of the core mental models of modern design systems. It gives us a common language for describing the interface as a hierarchy: atoms, molecules, organisms, templates, and pages.

Brad Frost said from the very beginning that atomic design is not a linear process, but a mental model that allows us to keep both the whole and its parts in view at the same time. The five levels are not steps one through five.

From Template to Atoms.

However, in practice, most teams apply the model in one direction. This is especially true when they aim to build a component library: they define the smallest reusable parts and assemble larger blocks from them. And the begin to use them all in screens.

This habit is so common that many people mistake it for the methodology itself.

Product work usually starts from the other side — from the user experience. When we look at a screen, the first question isn’t “what components are used here,” but “what does the user need to do here?” How will they search, filter, compare, select, edit, and so on?

This is another entry point into the Atomic Design model. We could say that this is a “scope-first” approach.

A component-first approach can obscure the actual structure

A “component-first” approach usually begins with an inventory:

  • This is a button
  • This is an input
  • This is a badge
  • This is a table

There are two well-known methods that handle this very well: Brad Frost’s Interface Inventory and Nathan Curtis’s Component Cut-Up Workshop. Both are excellent for their intended purpose: describing an existing interface and kicking off the work on the component library.

  • Interface Inventory
  • The Component Cut-Up Workshop

But they answer a specific question: “what’s on the screen?” We need to think about the rest ourselves: ”why something is there and what it’s connected to”.

Let’s take a typical admin screen with a data table as an example.

The user inventory here looks pretty good:

  • Page title
  • Primary actions
  • Tab navigation
  • Search input
  • Filter inputs
  • Sort buttons
  • Pagination
  • Tooltips
  • etc.

What remains behind the scenes is how all of this is interconnected:

  • The status badge is associated with a single row.
  • Sorting rearranges all rows in the dataset. Even though the control itself is located within a single column header.
  • Search and filters change which records are displayed on the screen at all.
  • A primary action like Add people affects the entire page.
  • Tabs can completely replace the content area’s contents.

The proximity of elements to one another is a poor guide in all of this. The sort button is the most obvious example: it resides in a column header but affects the entire table. Elements are linked not by their location, but by the scope of their behavior.

Thinking in scopes

When breaking down a screen, we can start with the scope of each action — the set of data or part of the interface that changes when the user triggers that action.

For the admin screen above:

This isn’t a complete breakdown, but it already highlights a couple of important points.

First: each row in the left column answers the same question — what is changing?

You might be tempted to add categories like “navigation” or “table header,” but these describe what the control is or where it’s located. That’s a different axis, and mixing the two axes is exactly what will cause the exercise to quietly turn back into an inventory breakdown.

Second: tooltips and badges have no scope at all. They don’t change anything. They’re included in the table to indicate that something isn’t a control — just to complete the picture.

This breakdown isn’t universal. On a different screen or in a different product, the scopes will be different.

It’s not the list that’s carried over, but the process:

  • Start with what the user can do and what they can interact with.
  • Determine what each specific user action will affect.
  • Decide which level should own the logic.

This way, we get a structural model of the screen even before we start creating components.

Where the logic lives

When we design components, we think about the library: its versatility, independence, and applicability in contexts we cannot predict.

When we design a product, we think about business logic — the parts must come together to form a cohesive user experience.

Search, filters, and pagination illustrate this tension quite clearly. As library components, they can appear in different combinations on different screens, so it makes sense to keep them independent.

But on this admin screen, they manage a shared dataset:

  • Changing a filter can reset pagination to the first page.
  • A search query with no matches empties the table, and pagination becomes unnecessary.

It is impossible to list all such scenarios when documenting individual components, and the components themselves should not be aware of them. The moment the filter component becomes aware of the pagination component, it loses its reusability and begins to carry the business logic of a single specific use case.

But something has to manage these connections. In my experience, it’s most convenient to do this at the template level.

A slightly different view on the role of a template

In Atomic Design, templates are page-level objects that position components within a layout and define the content structure: they are about structure, not state.

To put it very simply, a template acts as a “dumb” (presentational) component that only knows how it looks and what data it receives from outside.

“Smart components” (container components) are capable of managing data, state, and behavior. They are often built as wrappers around “dumb” (presentational) components.

This is roughly what I suggest doing with templates. The individual components remain “presentational”: a table knows how to render rows, a filter knows how to return a value, pagination knows how to display a page number — and they’re all independent and unaware of each other. The template is the wrapper that unites them and holds the logic for how they work together.

For data-dense product screens, the template level is the natural place not only for layout, but also for:

  • Which zones are on the screen and where they are located.
  • How the zones are connected.
  • The shared state that flows between them.
  • Rules that belong to the screen’s context, rather than to any specific component.

I have often seen developers on product teams create wrappers around several library components when they need to reuse the same set of features, such as filters, search, tables, and pagination, that behave as a single unit.

Of course, this kind of logic can be documented as a story in Storybook, but developers often prefer to keep it as ready-made modules rather than rebuilding it from scratch every time.

Sometimes these wrappers appear spontaneously and end up somewhere in the /components directory alongside buttons and other “presentational” components. However, it’s still better to keep such templates separate.

I should clarify: I’m not saying that every template must contain logic or that any logic should be dragged into a template. The criteria are the same as the question about scope:

  • If a rule describes a relationship between areas and is repeated from screen to screen (“changing the filter resets pagination to the first page”), it belongs in a template.
  • If a rule applies to a specific screen and specific data (“disabled users cannot change their role”), that’s at the page level, and the template shouldn’t be touched.

A template that knows too much stops being reusable.

I believe this is more of an extension than a contradiction to the logic of Atomic Design templates. This is also the clearest distinction between this approach and Component Cut-Up:

  • Cut-up helps the team identify recurring visual elements and turn them into a list of potential components.
  • A scope-first analysis helps understand “what a user can do on the screen, what their actions affect, and which level should be responsible for it”.

Same template, different reality

A good template is a reusable structure that works across different product contexts. For example, the same template can be used to manage Members, Projects, Invoices, and other pages.

The zones remain the same:

  • Page header
  • Primary action area
  • Navigation
  • Toolbar
  • Content area

What changes are the elements within them: same structure, different content and behavior.

This is the moment when a design system becomes more than just a set of components and begins to describe product patterns. This is exactly what most product teams need.

Checking the breakdown with real content

At the page level, we populate the templates with actual content. At this stage, we need to stress test the system and our layout to make sure the structure can handle content it might not have been designed for. Not just for the “happy path,” but also when:

  • When there is no data. For example, when a search query returns no results.
  • While data is loading.
  • When the page opens on a small screen.
  • The text is much longer than intended for the layout.

These are just a few scenarios for a particular single screen. Some of them are typical, such as the empty state. Others may be specific. It’s similar to what QA does with edge cases: finding where things break.

The difference lies in what “breaking” means. It’s not always a design problem. Often, it’s a sign that the breakdown is incomplete: a certain state or part of it has no owner, or a rule hasn’t been defined for the zone in case it’s empty.

When this approach is useful?

First, when you need to create a design system for an existing product. When the product already exists, the question isn’t “How do we create components from scratch?” but rather “How do we understand and systematize what already exists?”

Second, when there are debates about the boundaries of components. A scope-first breakdown provides both sides with a more neutral way to discuss ownership. Instead of arguing about whether something “looks like” a component, the team can discuss what it affects and which level should own that behavior.

Third, when a product has many similar screens. Admin panels, dashboards, CRM tools, settings pages, marketplaces, financial tools, and internal platforms often repeat the same patterns with different data. Scope-first approach helps clarify which parts are truly reusable and which are simply visually similar.

And finally — documentation. Product patterns are much easier to describe in terms of their scopes — page actions, object actions, states. Not through a flat list of components. And this is closer to how a user perceives the screen.

When this approach doesn’t help?

This approach isn’t one-size-fits-all, and based on my experience, I can point out at least two ways to mess it up.

The first is to adjust the logic and components to fit a single screen. The temptation is understandable: if the scope model just fits perfectly, you may want to build a library around it. But a screen is a specific use case, while components should live longer. A scope indicates the level at which the logic should reside. It says nothing about how versatile the component itself will be. I’ve encountered this situation very often when product teams were working under pressure, and designers and developers tried to save every new pattern as a component or a design system template.

The second is breaking down what’s already clear. On a landing page, settings form, or login screen, the scope map takes up a single line, yet it can still take a long time to analyze. The entire approach rests on two things: screen density and the overall flow between zones. If neither is present, a traditional inventory cut-up will be faster and deliver the exact same result.

Conclusion

Atomic Design is a versatile model that makes it quite easy to build component libraries. However, teams often try to use it to build interfaces from small parts, taking the “atomicity” of the approach too literally.

Day-to-day product work often starts from the other end: a complex screen already exists, and it needs to be understood. This article shows that Atomic Design helps with this as well. Moreover, the result is not just a more precise breakdown into components, but also a clearer understanding of the product pattern behind the screen.

For product teams, this is usually what matters most.

Thanks for reading! Write in the comments what you think about the topic.

Let’s stay in touch! Connect with me on LinkedIn and follow me here on Medium for more design-related content.

title: Supersonic dreams: how post-war France invented the future, and then stopped
text:
Supersonic dreams: how post-war France invented the future, and then stopped

Concorde, nuclear power and Minitel took three different paths. What can they tell us about Europe’s next technological bets?

I’ve spent the last week walking the streets of Marseille, indulging in my long-desired vacation. My routine was simple and mostly included booking tables at local spots, open for unapologetically short hours. A sense of urgency is a funny concept when applied anywhere in southern Europe. Born & raised in a southern European city, I can really say that.

At the Airbnb where I am staying, the skyline is surprisingly busy. The dense, almost panoptical view makes me think about an interesting thing. I wonder whether the atmosphere that I would describe as “clinically relaxed” was different in the past.

France in the 1970s was just peak. Unlike today, it was leaping ahead on a bunch of different tracks where bold vision, execution speed and big capital mattered. It was a tight race, and the French were taking the corners perfectly, often taking the lead over the Soviets and Americans.

https://medium.com/media/314577821abd2d41fb53a0dda13aa52f/href

The thirty years after WW2 are widely known as Trente Glorieuses or “Three Glorious Decades”. Of course, this era was not as perfect as French history documentaries may portray it. France went through a fair share of political crises when re-establishing itself politically, as well as a couple of ugly (post-)colonial wars. Yet eventually, long-lasting peace and transatlantic partnerships finally gave the continent the time and security needed for generational moonshots.

Unlike Germany, which was torn in two and heavily destroyed, France enjoyed a more pleasant type of integration and the luxury of deciding its own destiny. That included nationalising critical industries, obtaining nuclear arms and racing towards the edge of technological success.

By the late 1970s and early 1980s, French advancements were just bold. One of the quickest nuclear build-ups in history laid the foundations of French energy independence that endure to this day. Minitel — a French version of the internet, before the World Wide Web took over. And of course, a symbol of the supersonic dream: Concorde. Three bold bets on the future. One became a luxury, one became infrastructure, and one became obsolete.

Concorde: ahead of time

If there were ever a thing that I’d be willing to blow an unreasonable amount of money on immediately — it would be a Concorde flight. As a kid with parents in aviation, I am not easily surprised by anything flying, yet Concorde is something different.

Technically, it wasn’t all French: the two manufacturing facilities were located in Britain and France. That required a lot of coordination and joint effort, yet the French were never shy about taking credit for it.

The plane itself was incredibly sophisticated. There was a mechanism for changing the position of the nose section on every take-off and landing to give the pilots a clear view of the runway. Flying at supersonic speeds made the outer surface so hot that the whole plane would actually extend by tens of centimetres during the flight. Also, fuel would be pumped from one tank to another mid-flight to balance Concorde’s centre of gravity.

Concorde could let you beat the clock. With a flight time of around three and a half hours and New York five hours behind London, you could leave at noon and arrive at 10:30 am local time. The whole idea of stitching together the two sides of the Atlantic with a fast-track channel in the air was futurism in reality, a testament to post-war prosperity and a true European “Ad Astra” moment.

The cabin was narrow, with just four seats across. Yet it was still a more prestigious flight, with Champagne, caviar and a certificate for breaking the sound barrier. Passengers would sit next to the tiny windows and enjoy watching the plane reach a supersonic speed of Mach 2 live on the built-in indicators. In the 1990s, designer Andrée Putman redesigned Air France’s cabin, using light and restrained details to make the small space feel elegant.

Celebrities loved Concorde. No private jet could match the vibe of a cutting-edge aviation unit, leaping forth ahead of its time. Among its passengers were Mick Jagger, Paul McCartney, Catherine Deneuve and, of course, members of the British royal family.

The final flight of Concorde took place on November 26, 2003, when it flew to Filton for preservation. Commercial services had ended the previous month. Its demise had no single cause. Instead, it was a mix of circumstances, including the famous jet crash of 2000, a shrinking market and rising maintenance costs. The oil crisis of 1973 had already made the economics of supersonic travel harder, long before the final retirement. Add to this a limited number of routes (sonic booms restricted supersonic flying over land) and you get the reason why Concorde became a piece of the future that was no longer economically viable.

Nuclear: an atomic ramp-up

Back in Marseille, I’m pulling out my phone, which I’ve set to a radical “do not disturb” mode, to check the map, as we’re heading to the beach. One of the push notifications that somehow invades my attention span is about upcoming spikes in energy costs. I put my sunglasses away to figure out the route and instinctively dive into noisy news blurbs, wondering if my electricity bill is gonna hurt after I’m back home in Berlin.

My electricity bill might be lower if I decided to settle in France. Energy price shocks are hardly new to the French. Back in the seventies, France already had a nuclear industry when oil prices skyrocketed. The crisis then pushed the country to accelerate its reactor build-out.

The idea of strategic autonomy and the notion of self-sustaining politics were cornerstones of post-war France. This was the reason why such assertiveness in both the military and civilian parts of the economy was taken to a higher level. Ironically enough, the heart of the nuclear programme ran on American hardware. France had already built reactors of its own design, but chose a different technology for the expansion. In 1969, the final decision to use PWRs under a Westinghouse licence was reached. Later on, the reactors were adapted and “franced” — by the 1980s, production had achieved a reasonable degree of local autonomy.

The build-out itself was carried out in the same manner as all the other post-war transformations: centralised, strategic, massive. EDF (Électricité de France) was basically the state-owned national utility. To fund its enormous effort, it was authorised to borrow enormous sums. The amount of borrowed capital was so huge that by 1976, EDF was the third-biggest borrower on the US capital market — right after Ford and General Motors.

Make no mistake — France did not predict the oil crisis, nor did it slide through it. At the time, the energy price spikes did really bite. Yet in March of 1974, when then-prime minister Pierre Messmer announced an acceleration of the build-out, there was infrastructure in place to be accelerated.

The build-up wasn’t flawless: the speed and the directive manner backfired, sparking various protests across the country. One major flashpoint was Superphénix — a new form of reactor that ran on the principle of “fast” neutrons and used a much newer and more experimental technology. Yet it wasn’t the only thing people were mad about.

It was the non-consensual policy that made people angry: both intellectuals and the working class from rural areas. Specifically, this happened at Plogoff, near Pointe du Raz, where EDF was planning a four-reactor nuclear power station. The locals viewed this as a risk of land expropriation and disruption to fishing. Soon enough, the protests spun out of control, and after years of tension, the project was called off in 1981.

Nuclear power was probably France’s most successful 1970s bet. Energy security drove the programme; lower-carbon electricity became another lasting benefit. Yet it became a backbone of the country’s autonomy and reduced volatility & external dependence, setting France apart from its neighbours.

To this day, French power plants are monuments to Cold War-era futurism that actually became part of the economy and didn’t disappear. And surprisingly, some of them look really nice for the industrial monstrosities those things are always considered to be. It could be the beautiful landscape around them that is doing the job, or the more elegant architecture the French are famous for. But probably both.

Minitel: online before the web

I’m trying to get a table at Le Ventre de l’Architecte at the famous Le Corbusier house. The opening hours are wild: 12–2 pm, 7:30–9:15 pm, meaning you’d better get hungry when the place is open. After reading a bunch of unhinged comments from the restaurant manager (check their reviews on Google, it’s just fire), I navigate to the website. As a person who led a premium web studio, I am disappointed but not surprised by what I see. A question that pops up in my mind: was the French internet any good?

Spoiler: hell yes.

When we think about the early days of the internet and picture its mass adoption, we immediately imagine the US. Yet France brought online services into millions of homes well before the web became an everyday habit.

Minitel was a European predecessor of the World Wide Web. It kicked off at the beginning of the 1980s. As a telephone subscriber, you could get one of the Minitel terminals for free. This wouldn’t be a regular PC: no apps or games on the device, just a b&w text interface for online services. Its design had practical limits: screen designer Jean-Yves Michalik described the 40-column display and an alphabetic keyboard that was later replaced with AZERTY.

Minitel terminals were originally a fancy replacement for the paper directory. People would get hooked on additional functions like purchasing train tickets or making bookings pretty randomly, after their usual phone number searches. Apparently, this was a great strategy for adoption: by 1989, France had around five million Minitel terminals. By 1993, that figure had grown to almost 6.5 million, with terminals in 20% of households.

https://medium.com/media/32699826694b1587b4b4312597f62cc3/href

Minitel was no random accident. It was part of a visionary digital transformation, imagined, described and delivered by the French state in order to bring a futuristic reality into everyday life. “The Computerisation of Society”, a report that came out in 1978, explored the emergence of an information society. The report contained a blueprint of how the mass adoption of computers would shift many gears in societal interaction, how business would change and how politics would follow. It also considered the infrastructure and political choices that this transformation would require.

That report captured the ambition behind France’s push into networked computing.

One of the things Minitel would give birth to was anonymous dating chats. Or, as they called them, “pink chats”. Users would assume they were speaking with someone who was who they said they were, which was not always the case.

Minitel’s early success did not turn into global dominance. Its dedicated terminals and centrally organised network made online services accessible, but eventually faced competition from personal computers and the open web. An OECD assessment pointed to ageing technology, high usage charges and limited export markets. The system that had made getting online simple also had limits.

The last official year of Minitel was 2012. That was a surprisingly long life for a network born at the beginning of the 1980s.

Nowadays: winds of European tech sovereignty

One thing that caught my eye in Marseille was how many things are called “Mistral”, from navy ships you can see docked in the harbour to local soda brands and driving schools that have this word in their name.

It’s a special, even holy word for many francophones. Mistral is the name of a strong, cold & mighty Mediterranean wind that blows all across Provence.

Also, Mistral is the name of one of the few European frontier AI labs. As I write this text, the fourth generation of its Large model has been announced, adding another chapter to France’s ambitions in computing.

It’s too early to predict whether the new European bet on open-weight sovereign models and an application layer for robotics and manufacturing will win the future.

But at least we know that writing the future was once in fashion in Europe.
Why not again?

Further reading

  • British Airways: Celebrating Concorde — the aircraft and its service history.
  • Andrée Putman: Le Concorde Air France — the cabin redesign.
  • IAEA: France country profile — the nuclear programme and reactor choices.
  • Archives départementales du Finistère: Plogoff — the proposed plant and opposition.
  • OECD: Minitel assessment — adoption, economics and limitations.
  • Jean-Yves Michalik: Minitel screen design — a contemporary practitioner’s account.

title: This Is The Best (And Most Romantic) Way To Get To Know Your Partner While Traveling
text:
This Is The Best (And Most Romantic) Way To Get To Know Your Partner While Traveling

I’m headed into the second year of my relationship, and I’m still getting to know my boyfriend. After more than five vacations together, I know we’re both up early, always down to explore, and very serious about trying new restaurants wherever we’re staying. But there are still stories from his past I haven’t heard and questions I haven’t thought to ask.  

That curiosity has been part of our relationship from the beginning. When we first started dating, I brought out conversation cards to help us get to know each other beyond the usual get-to-know-you icebreaker questions. Those questions gave us a place to start conversations that might not have come up on their own. They helped us get comfortable sharing more of ourselves, and the cards became something we both enjoyed. Now, sometimes he’s the one suggesting we pull out the cards.  

One thing I cherish about our relationship is how well we travel together. So, when The Skin Deep and Secrets Resorts & Spas invited us to Mexico to experience their partnership, it felt like a trip made for us. I was already familiar with The Skin Deep and its work exploring human connection, but I hadn’t realized the company also made conversation card games. The collaboration with Secrets is a limited-edition Away, Together Conversation Card Game that encourages couples to slow down and get to know each other more deeply, while on vacation.  

The resort had plenty of dining and activity options to keep us occupied, so laying on the beach and dinner became our opportunity to pull out The Skin Deep cards. We’d sit down to eat, start asking questions, and let the conversation go wherever it took us. One question stayed with me: “What is the pain in me you wish you could heal and why?” We’re still relatively early in our relationship, but we’ve already shared enough for that question to mean something. Answering it meant thinking back to the moments when we’d opened up to each other, the things we’d heard, and what had stayed with us. It made me reflect on how closely we were listening, and how much we understood about what the other person carries.

Another question that made us think: “Ten years from now, how do you think our vacations are going to differ and what do you hope remains the same?” My answer came pretty quickly: a lot more kids. He already has a six-year-old daughter, and we’ve talked about having children together, so I can definitely see more family vacations in our future. Our trips might require a little more planning and a few more suitcases, but I hope our love for travel stays the same. Even with more responsibilities and life looking different, I hope we’re still excited to see the world, experience other cultures, and try something new together. I’d love for our kids to grow up sharing that curiosity, too.

My boyfriend even admitted that The Skin Deep questions helped him be more communicative. That surprised me because, in our relationship, he’s always been willing to play along, answer, and sometimes initiate the game himself. I wouldn’t have known that opening up hadn’t always come naturally to him. Hearing that made me appreciate the habit we’d started early on even more. That’s what made this partnership feel so natural to our experience. The cards gave us a new direction to take the conversation in, and being away gave us the time to stay with the answers and really go deeper with each other. 

Going into our second year, I want us to keep making room for that curiosity at home, too. I love how well we know each other already, and I love that there’s still so much left to ask. For now, we’ll keep pulling out the cards. 

Sandy Pierre is the Branded Execution Manager at Refinery29 Unbothered and a contributing writer covering travel, lifestyle, and culture. When she’s not working on brand partnerships, she’s probably planning her next trip or curating a dinner for creatives in New York.

title: My New Fav Charlotte Tilbury Products Are On Sale For Amazon’s Holiday Beauty Haul
text:
My New Fav Charlotte Tilbury Products Are On Sale For Amazon’s Holiday Beauty Haul

As a shopping writer, there are few times when I’m actually repurchasing makeup, typically trying a revolving door of new products instead. But, there’s one beauty item that I use until the very last drop and immediately re-order: Charlotte Tilbury’s Big Lip Plumpgasm. It’s the perfect plumping lip gloss that gets me endless compliments. And now lucky for me (and you), it’s currently on sale during Amazon’s Holiday Beauty Haul Event! But there’s even more of my favorite Charlotte Tilbury goodies to score limited-time deals on.

I recently attended a Charlotte Tilbury masterclass hosted by Amazon, where we got to try tons of OG and new products while re-creating Christina Aguilera’s holiday campaign glam, taught by makeup artist Alex Rutkovskiy. While there were so many exciting products that I tried, I wanted to spotlight the ones on sale (so you can get the most bang for your buck and stock up on holiday gifts), plus share Rutkovskiy’s application tips to get the prettiest, glowiest glam this season.

Charlotte Tilbury offers a holiday cracker kit filled with the brand’s most popular Pillow Talk shade products, including the Beauty Light Wand, Lip Cheat liner, and Plumpgasm. “Pillow Talk started as one shade of lipstick,” Rutkovskiy explained, joking: “Charlotte selfishly created her personal lip color. And it’s the number one bestseller in the world.” Today, Pillow Talk has multiple iterations so everyone can enjoy it: Fair, Original, Medium, and Deep.

And right now, this makeup set is selling for under $25 on Amazon in both Pillow Talk and Super Nude, making it a great beauty kit refresh and even better stocking stuffer.

For the highlighter, which comes in seven shades (all on sale!), Rutkovskiy likes applying it to his hand first and warming it up with a brush. He then adds it to the high points of the face, like the cheekbones, nose, cupid’s bow, and chin before applying extra product with his fingertips. “It helps to layer it. It looks very healthy and glowy with more dimension. Charlotte is the queen of the glow, so we love a glowing face.” (He also called out how influencers complain about the packaging exploding in their makeup bags and purses, but that there’s a simple open-and-close twist applicator. The more you know!)

The kit also features the ultimate lip combo, IMO: Lip Cheat and Plumpgasm. Rutkovskiy taught us Charlotte Tilbury’s signature heart-shaped lip, first over-lining the cupid’s bow and center of the bottom lip. Then, you can connect the sides of your lips from the corners to the center for a lifting effect, rather than dragging down your lips.

We also applied the brand’s Matte Revolution Lipstick in Pillow Talk with a lip brush, which isn’t so much of a requirement for me. While that lip product isn’t on sale on Amazon, the creamier K.I.S.S.I.N.G Lipstick is if you want an Aguilera-esque pout.

And the final step was my Holy Grail (aka lip gloss). Speaking on Plumpgasm, Rutkovskiy said: “There’s people who hate plumping glosses and people who are obsessed with them, and there’s no one in the middle.” He added: “It’s such a beautiful formula, which combines heat and cool ingredients, so there’s pepper and mint. It’s cold and hot at the same time. And it plumps your lips in the first three minutes.” Rutkovskiy predominantly keeps the gloss at the center of the lips for extra dimension, but I definitely dowse my lips in the spicy, juicy formula, especially for late-night plans and holiday parties.

Note: If you aren’t sold on all three products in the kit, you can find the Beauty Light Wand highlighter and Plumpgasm lip gloss sold separately and on sale too!

title: I Wore Samsung’s Galaxy Watch9 For 30 Days To Keep Myself Accountable
text:
I Wore Samsung’s Galaxy Watch9 For 30 Days To Keep Myself Accountable

If you’re like us, you’ve talked yourself out of a lot of good decisions, and into a few bad ones, because you couldn’t tell what was actually worth it. VETTED is here to help. Whether it’s a product, a procedure, or a place, we do the digging, ask the real questions, and try it ourselves before we tell you a thing. If it made the cut, it’s because it earned it.

I’m finally taking my fitness journey and my health seriously, and I’m learning that the best way to hold myself accountable is to actually track my progress. So when Samsung’s Galaxy Watch9 came out, I was interested in trying it for at least 30 days to see how if it could fit into my life and show me real-time results of how I was doing in my health journey. 

The Product 

The Galaxy Watch9 is Samsung’s smartwatch for tracking everyday activity, workouts, and sleep. It has a slim profile and feels very light on my wrist, which I appreciated while wearing it throughout the day.  

In addition to fitness features, the watch offers wellness tools including Vitals and a Heart Health Score. For me, the appeal was having more information about my routine in one place, without needing to become a fitness expert to start paying attention.  

How I Used It 

My first order of business was tracking my steps. My personal goal was 10,000 a day, and being able to look at my wrist and see where I stood. I could easily check my progress throughout the day instead of guessing how much walking I’d done. 

But then I found myself tracking more than that. I checked my daily activity, workouts, estimated calories burned, heart-related metrics, cycle, and sleep patterns. I went into the month focused on movement and ended up using the watch to keep tabs on more of my overall wellness. 

What I Noticed 

I’m the type of person who needs to see progress to stay consistent. Having my activity right there on a screen gave me something tangible to check in with. The watch let me know when I hadn’t moved enough and offered encouragement when I was making progress.  

I also appreciated that it picked up activities like jogging and swimming without me having to manually start tracking every time. That made it easier to focus on what I was doing. 

 I will admit, sometimes I wouldn’t wear it all the time. There were nights I forgot to put it on before bed and times I made it to the gym without it. Usually, I’d take it off because it didn’t go with my outfit or because I wanted to shower without it, then I’d forget to put it back on. 

The Price 

The Galaxy Watch9 starts at $379.99 for the Bluetooth model, with the price varying by size and connectivity. For the way I used it, I think it’s worth its value.  

I’ve paid more for things I barely touched more than once. A watch that helps me keep up with goals I’m actively working toward feels easier to justify. The value, for me, comes from how often I reach for it and use the information it gives me. 

Would I Buy It Myself? 

Yes. While this watch was gifted, after 30 days of using it, I would spend my own money on it. 

This was my introduction to being a Samsung girl, and I get the hype. I was impressed by how much information I could keep track of, just from my wrist. More than anything, it fit a need I already had: a way to see my activity and hold myself accountable as I work on being more consistent. 

Who It’s For 

This watch makes sense for someone who likes seeing their progress, wants a digital accountability partner, or is figuring out how to make wellness a more regular part of their life. You don’t need to be training for a marathon to use this watch. I started with a daily step goal. 

Phone compatibility matters, too. Check that your phone supports the watch and the features you want before buying; certain tools, including Vitals, require a compatible Samsung Galaxy phone.  

The Verdict 

For me, the Galaxy Watch9 is worth it. Over those 30 days, it made it easier to see what I was doing and where I needed to be more consistent. The movement reminders and automatic workout recognition were especially helpful because they gave me support without requiring me to manage every detail. 

I’m still responsible for getting my steps in, going to the gym, and putting the watch back on after getting dressed, but having a way to track those efforts has been useful enough that I want to keep wearing it beyond the 30-day period. 

I’m proud of myself for setting a challenge and sticking to it. Now, I’m already looking for new bands. If it’s going to be part of my daily routine, I want it to work with the outfit, too.
